clue.text: Flipped over, part of landscape so perfect lay still

indicators.note: something flipped over lies the other way round, so the hidden run is read backwards
only a part of the following words is wanted, a run of letters sitting across the word boundaries

parts.note: the run spanning the end of 'landscape', all of 'so' and the start of 'perfect'

explanation.surface: A picture-perfect landscape seen upside down, as if someone lay in the grass gazing at it.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden letters run backwards across 'landscaPE SO PERfect', giving REPOSE. Here 'lay still' is a noun phrase in disguise: repose is rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Repose means a state of rest or calm, which is what anyone who lay still would be enjoying; treat the phrase as describing that restful condition.

clue.text: Start of road rage connected with 4x4

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of 'road' is kept

parts.note: first letter of 'road'
rage and anger are synonyms
over = concerning, connected with, as in 'a row over money'

explanation.surface: A driver loses their temper on the road, somehow tied up with a big off-roader.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface welds 'road rage' into one phrase, but the two words do separate jobs. 'Connected with' is used in its sense of about or concerning, as in 'a row over money'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Range Rover is a well-known British brand of four-wheel-drive vehicle, and 4x4 is the everyday label for such cars.

clue.text: 12 who's out with a part to play in exercise

indicators.note: the article and the part sit in the exercise abbreviation, which wraps around them

parts.note: PE = physical education, school exercise
the article as printed
an actor's part is a role

explanation.surface: A released offender given a part in a keep-fit session.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 across is CRIMINAL, so the definition reads 'criminal who's out'. PE (physical education) is the school name for exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: A parolee is a convicted prisoner released early on conditions, so a lawbreaker who is out of jail but still supervised.

clue.text: Sorry rogues divided by start of case, cause of distress

indicators.note: a thing divided by something has that something driven into it
a sorry state is a poor, broken one, so the rogues are knocked out of shape

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only the opening of 'case' is kept

parts.note: first letter of 'case'

explanation.surface: Villains split up by a court case, which ends up a source of misery.
explanation.walkthrough: ROGUES rearranged gives SOURGE, and C is pushed in after the S. 'Sorry' looks like an apology but is the rearranging instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourge is a whip, and by extension any affliction or persistent source of suffering, such as plague or famine.

clue.text: American biscuit, 12 11 with an excellent example

parts.note: 12 and 11 read 'criminal feller': the surname of Daniel, one of the two men convicted of cutting down the Sycamore Gap tree
British slang for a first-rate specimen, the same word as the Christmas novelty pulled with a bang

explanation.surface: A US snack paired with a lawbreaking lumberjack and a fine specimen.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle's theme is the felling of the Sycamore Gap tree on Hadrian's Wall in 2023; the two men convicted were Daniel Graham and Adam Carruthers. The answer continues at 18 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A graham cracker is a sweet wholemeal biscuit popular in the United States, the base of s'mores; Americans call biscuits crackers or cookies.

clue.text: Brute's sport fine and innocent? On the contrary

parts.note: RU = rugby union
F = fine, as on pencil leads

indicators.note: the contrary of a direction is its opposite, so the word for innocent runs backwards

parts.note: a naif is an innocent, unworldly person

explanation.surface: Is a thug's game clean and blameless? Quite the opposite, says the clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' reads like a retort to the question, but it only turns the innocent round. The 's after Brute just links definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruffian is a violent, lawless person, a thug; brute is a direct synonym for such a savage individual.

clue.text: Emperor enjoyed wet weather on island heading north

parts.note: to have had something is to have enjoyed it

indicators.note: in a down entry north is up, so the island letter moves one place higher inside the weather word

parts.words: wet weather on island heading north
parts.note: rain is wet weather; its I (island) is the letter that moves up

explanation.surface: A Roman ruler who liked a drizzly day on some isle, heading north (as he did to build his wall).
explanation.walkthrough: HAD RAIN nearly spells it; the I in RAIN moves up one square to give RIAN. Hadrian built the wall across northern England that 16 across completes as 6's 16.
explanation.definitionFit: Hadrian was the second-century Roman ruler of the empire who ordered the famous defensive wall across Britain.

clue.text: Duck answer, breaking scheme to work together?

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it, so the answer abbreviation goes into the scheme

parts.note: a merger is a plan for two firms to combine
ANS is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: An order to dodge, and an answer that wrecks a plan for cooperation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' reads as a verb telling you to dodge; it is the bird. The question mark flags that a merger is only loosely a scheme to work together.
explanation.definitionFit: The merganser is a fish-eating diving bird with a serrated bill, one of the sawbill species of wildfowl.

clue.text: Stupendous case of unbelievable morons horsing around

indicators.note: horsing around is fooling about, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of 'unbelievable' are wanted

parts.note: first and last letters of 'unbelievable'

explanation.surface: An astonishing instance of idiots messing about.
explanation.walkthrough: MORONS plus the outside letters of 'unbelievable' rearrange into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupendous means astonishingly large or impressive, and enormous means huge, so both describe something of vast size.

clue.text: Report of diseased leaf travellers picked up somewhere along 6's 16

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word for diseased is taken by its sound

parts.note: diseased = sick, spelt as it sounds

indicators.note: in a down entry, picking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a leaf of a book is a page
the Roma are a traditionally travelling people

explanation.surface: A dispatch about blighted foliage carried up by wanderers along the Roman wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diseased leaf' looks like one idea, a tree ailment, but 'leaf' belongs with 'travellers': PAGE ROMA read upwards. 6's 16 is Hadrian's Wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Sycamore Gap is a dip in Hadrian's Wall in Northumberland, famous for a lone tree illegally cut down in 2023.

clue.text: Editor probes social media sites for item on noodle

indicators.note: a probe goes inside something, so the editor ends up within the sites

parts.note: fora is a plural of forum, an online discussion site
ED is the usual short form of editor

explanation.surface: A journalist digs through online platforms looking for something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noodle' suggests pasta but is slang for the head, so an item on it is a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A fedora is a soft felt hat with a creased crown, and noodle is informal slang for the head it sits upon.

clue.text: Man of prominence in Cumbria? That's doubtful

parts.note: a fell is a hill or mountain in the Lake District of Cumbria, north-west England
er is the sound of hesitation or doubt

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man is important up in Cumbria, and is told probably not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of prominence' reads as a VIP, but prominence here is a hill. Feller also fits the theme: a feller of trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Feller is colloquial for fellow, an informal word for a man or chap in everyday speech.

clue.text: Miscreant caught at home between border and lake area the other way

indicators.note: the other way means in the opposite direction, so the lake and area letters are swapped round
something set between two things is enclosed by them, here by the border and the lake area

parts.note: c = caught, cricket scorecard shorthand
a rim is an edge or border
in = at home
L = lake, as on maps
A = area

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer is arrested at their house, somewhere between the frontier and the lakes.
explanation.walkthrough: The C stands outside the sandwich: only 'at home' sits between border and lake area, and the lake-area pair is turned round before it goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A miscreant is a wrongdoer or villain, and a criminal is a person who has broken the law.

clue.text: A male's been misrepresenting skilled hands

indicators.note: to misrepresent is to present wrongly, so the letters are put forward in the wrong order

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A man has been passing himself off as having expert handiwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' means crew members, as in 'all hands on deck', not the ends of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: Able seamen are qualified sailors in the navy, and hands is the traditional word for crew members aboard a ship.

clue.text: Silly gamble before 12 case, ultimately saying he did it?

indicators.note: a silly gamble is a foolish, jumbled one, so its letters are scrambled

parts.note: anagram fodder
am = ante meridiem, the hours before twelve noon

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of 'case' is used

parts.note: last letter of 'case'

explanation.surface: A foolish bet in a criminal trial, where each defendant points at the other.
explanation.walkthrough: The '12' looks like a cross-reference to CRIMINAL, but 'before 12' is AM, the morning. The two tree-fellers each blamed the other at trial.
explanation.definitionFit: The blame game is the idiom for mutual finger-pointing, each party accusing another of fault; 'he did it' is its typical line.

clue.text: Put away in silence after denial

parts.note: no is a denial
sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: Someone locked up and kept quiet after refusing to confess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' sounds like jailing, but it means eating heartily; 'in' merely joins the two halves of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To put away food is to eat plenty of it, and nosh is informal British slang for eating or food.

clue.text: Defence some 12 lawyers retracted

indicators.note: some of the words means just a portion of their letters, taken across the join
something retracted is drawn back, so the hidden run is read backwards

parts.note: 12 across is CRIMINAL, so the phrase is 'criminal lawyers', and the run spans its last letter and the first three of 'lawyers'

explanation.surface: A legal defence team backing down from the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defence' sounds legal next to lawyers, but it is a barrier. The hidden letters only appear once 12 is replaced by CRIMINAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A wall is a barrier built for protection, and Hadrian's is the obvious example of a fortification here.

clue.text: Like yobs, pleased after topping beauty

indicators.note: topping something cuts off its top, which in a down entry is the first letter of the word for pleased

parts.note: glad without its first letter
a dish is slang for an attractive person

explanation.surface: Hooligans delighted after beating a pretty contender.
explanation.walkthrough: GLAD loses its G. 'Topping' looks like an adjective (British for excellent) or a win, but it removes the top letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Laddish describes rowdy, boorish young-male behaviour, and yobs are loutish hooligans, the British word for such thugs.

clue.text: 12 11 — possibly 1D 23 tyre track belonging to them?

parts.note: 1 down with 23 is a Range Rover, one example of a car
a rut is a groove worn by wheels
hers is 'belonging to them' when them are women, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: A tree-felling criminal's getaway, told through the vehicle and its tracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 11 is 'criminal feller': Adam Carruthers, convicted with Daniel Graham of cutting down the Sycamore Gap tree. The pair drove a Range Rover to the site.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Carruthers was one of two men jailed for chopping down the famous Sycamore Gap tree, a lawbreaking tree-cutter.

clue.text: See 4
E.g. moors map held by police sergeant with uniform on

indicators.note: a thing held by others is gripped between them, here by the police rank together with its uniform letter

parts.note: U = uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a plan is a map or drawing
DS = detective sergeant

explanation.surface: A police officer in uniform holding a chart of the moorland they are searching.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so uniform goes on top of the sergeant, and the map is held inside that pair. 'E.g.' shows moors are one kind of upland.
explanation.definitionFit: Moors are high, open, uncultivated ground, an example of the higher terrain known collectively as uplands.

clue.text: Chap who follows what's trending cheers broadcast of cut tree

indicators.note: a cut word has lost its end, so the plant word drops its final letter

parts.note: hips as in 'hip, hip, hooray', the cheers of a crowd

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters seed widely, so the letters of the shortened plant are scattered

parts.note: tree without its last letter

explanation.surface: A trendy man applauding news coverage of a felled tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to the theme: the Sycamore Gap felling was broadcast everywhere. 'Cheers' is not a toast here but the hip-hip of applause.
explanation.definitionFit: A hipster is someone who keeps up with the latest fashions and fads, a devotee of what is currently cool.

clue.text: Suspect abed cutting string up? Nod vigorously

indicators.note: to cut into something is to go inside it, so the rearranged letters sit within the word for execute

parts.note: to string someone up is to hang them

indicators.note: something suspect is dodgy and not as it seems, so the bed word is rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A suspect in bed is about to be lynched, then someone nods hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' reads as a noun, a person under suspicion, but it is the rearranging instruction for ABED.
explanation.definitionFit: To headbang is to shake the head violently in time to loud rock or metal music, an energetic form of nodding.

clue.text: Social outcasts trapped by juvenile personalities

indicators.note: the answer is trapped inside the following words, held across their join

parts.note: the end of 'juvenile' and the start of 'personalities'

explanation.surface: Young characters shunned by their peers.
explanation.walkthrough: The run straddles juveniLE PERSonalities.
explanation.definitionFit: Leper is used figuratively for someone shunned by others, from the historical exclusion of people with leprosy.

clue.text: See 1
Town in the Borders that uncovered illuminating bit of string

indicators.note: uncovering strips the outside layer, so the first and last letters of 'that' are removed

parts.note: 'that' without its outer letters
a wick is the string in a candle that burns to give light

explanation.surface: A candle's burning thread reveals a place in southern Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Borders is the region of Scotland next to the English border. 'Uncovered' looks like 'revealed' but strips 'that' to its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawick is a textile town in the Scottish Borders council area, known for knitwear and rugby.

clue.text: Joke one has about it, meant as retribution

parts.note: a pun is a joke on words

indicators.note: to have something about you is to carry it around, so the contraction wraps the pronoun

parts.note: 'one has' in first-person contraction, I've

indicators.note: about also means turned round, as in about-face, so the pronoun is reversed

parts.note: the pronoun as printed

explanation.surface: Someone making a pun at another's expense, as a form of payback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' does two jobs here: it wraps 'one has' round 'it', and it also turns 'it' back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Punitive means intended to punish, and retribution is punishment inflicted in return for a wrong done.

clue.text: Former mate with brief wanting second counsel

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the word for brief loses its S for second

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
short without S, the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: An ex-partner, holding a legal brief, seeks a second barrister's opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' and 'counsel' both sound like lawyers, but brief is SHORT and counsel is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhort is to urge or advise someone strongly, and to counsel is likewise to give advice or recommend a course.

clue.text: One takes a great deal of interest, certainly, in what occupies jury

definitions.text: One takes a great deal of interest

indicators.note: the word for certainly goes in between the inner letters of the jury word
what occupies a word is its contents, the letters inside once the outer ones are gone

parts.note: the inner letters of 'jury'
sure = certainly

explanation.surface: A juror who is very interested in the case, certainly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interest' sounds like curiosity, but it is money charged on a loan.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money at exorbitant rates, so charging excessive interest on loans is the defining trade.
